ety.text: From Middle English licence, licens, lisence, lissens, licance, from Old French licence, from Latin licentia (“license”), from licens, present participle of licere (“to be allowed, be allowable”); compare linquere, Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave”).
From Middle English licencen, licensen, lisensen, licent, from Old French licencer, licencier, licenciier, licenser, from Medieval Latin licentiō (cf. English licentiate).

senses.d: A legal document giving official permission to do something; a permit.
ex: Hello. I would like to buy a fish licence please.

senses.d: The legal terms under which a person is allowed to use a product, especially software.
Freedom to deviate deliberately from normally applicable rules or practices (especially in behaviour or speech).
Excessive freedom; lack of due restraint.
ex:
I envy not the beast that takes
⁠His license in the field of time,
⁠Unfetter’d by the sense of crime,
To whom a conscience never wakes; […]
When liberty becomes license dictatorship is near.

senses.d: To authorize officially.
ex: I am licensed to practice law in this state.

senses.d: To give formal authorization to use.
ex: It was decided to license Wikipedia under the GFDL.

senses.d: To acquire authorization to use, usually in exchange for compensation.
ex: The filmmakers licensed several iconic 80's songs for the soundtrack.
As part of the strategic relationship, Microsoft has licensed the image segmentation, compression and viewing technology from ScanSoft.

senses.d: To give permission or freedom to; accept.
To permit (as grammatically correct).
ex: No English adverbs have mandatory complements, and most don't even license optional ones.

grp.label: legal document giving official permission to do something
to give formal authorization to use

ety.text: Inherited from Old French licence, borrowed from Latin licentia.

pt:licença.gl: license; permit (legal document giving official permission to do something)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese lecença, from Latin licentia (“license; freedom; liberty”), from licēns (“allowing, permitting”), present participle of licet (“allow”).

senses.d: The act by which something is licked.
A severe beating.
A great loss or defeat.
ex: Our football team took a licking last night.

senses.d: Having been issued with a licence (by the required authority).
ex: Only licensed exterminators can purchase rat poison in this state.

senses.d: Allowed to sell alcohol.
ex: The opening hours of licensed premises are restricted to prevent all-night drinking.

senses.d: Authorized by licence.
ex: Even licensed fishing has a major effect on the fish population in the river.

senses.d: Based on an existing piece of intellectual property and sold under licence.
ex: Although they sell well, licensed video games are seldom critically acclaimed.

grp.label: having been issued with a license

senses.d: A giving of license to do something; sanction.

ety.text: From Middle English likken, from Old English liccian, from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Sense evolution towards violence unclear; not paralleled in any other Germanic language.
Back-formation from hit a lick, which see. Ultimately from liquor.

senses.d: To stroke with the tongue.
ex: The cat licked its fur.

senses.d: To lap; to take in with the tongue.
ex: She licked the last of the honey off the spoon before washing it.
Jim closed his eyes and licked his vanilla ice cream cone.

senses.d: To beat with repeated blows.
To defeat decisively, particularly in a fight.
ex: My dad can lick your dad.

senses.d: To overcome.
ex: I think I can lick this.

senses.d: To perform cunnilingus.
To do anything partially.
To lap.
The act of licking; a stroke of the tongue.
ex: The cat gave its fur a lick.

senses.d: The amount of some substance obtainable with a single lick.
ex: Give me a lick of ice cream.

senses.d: A quick and careless application of anything, as if by a stroke of the tongue.
ex: a lick of paint
to put on colours with a lick of the brush

senses.d: A place where animals lick minerals from the ground.
ex: The birds gathered at the clay lick.

senses.d: A small watercourse or ephemeral stream. It ranks between a rill and a stream.
ex: We used to play in the lick.

senses.d: A stroke or blow.
ex: Hit that wedge a good lick with the sledgehammer.
I went in big licks, and, although it was a good-sized pile, I chopped it all up before he got back at night.

senses.d: A small amount; a whit.
ex: You don't have a lick of sense.
I didn't do a lick of work today.

senses.d: An attempt at something.
A short motif.
ex: There are some really good blues licks in this solo.

senses.d: A rate of speed. (Always qualified by good, fair, or a similar adjective.)
ex: The bus was travelling at a good lick when it swerved and left the road.

senses.d: An instance or opportunity to earn money fast, usually by illegal means, thus a heist, drug deal etc. or its victim; mostly used in phrasal verbs: hit a lick, hit licks
ex: Bitch, pig, pull out with the stick / everything I hit like a lick / We don’t miss
You see a lick and you rob him / I see a lick then I stop on the block and I pause him

grp.label: to lap, to take in with the tongue

ety.text: From Middle French lecher, from Old French lechier, from a Vulgar Latin *liccāre (compare Italian leccare), itself probably from Frankish *likkōn. See English lick for more. Alternatively from an early contraction of *ligicāre, denasalized from *lingicāre, from Classical Latin lingere.

From a Vulgar Latin *liccāre (compare French lécher), itself probably from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn. See English lick for more. Alternatively from an early contraction of *ligicāre, denasalized from *lingicāre, from Classical Latin lingere.

fr:défaire.gl: to take down, take apart, dismantle, unpack (luggage)

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French desfaire, from Old French desfaire, from Early Medieval Latin disfacere. Synchronically dé- + faire.

Inherited from Old French veintre, later veincre, vencre, inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, nasal infix from *weyk- (“to overcome”). The current pronunciation is influenced by the first-person singular indicative present form vincō. Compare also Spanish vencer.
Perhaps of African origin; compare Proto-Bantu *kɪ̀ntʊ̀ (“little thing, small object”).
